e.t: Abraam is a proper name referring to the biblical person known as Abraham. It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, the name appears 201 times, with most occurrences in Genesis and other Old Testament books. The supplied renderings preserve the name as “Abraam” or “Avraam,” showing that it functions as a personal designation throughout this corpus.

Agar is a proper name referring to the woman known as Agar in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is carried by the individual who bears the name. The word appears 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical corpus, most often in Genesis 16. It is also found once in Baruch.3.23.

This noun means “arrogance”: an attitude of proud self-importance that treats oneself as superior or above proper limits. It names a settled quality or posture rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs three times, in Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse text is needed to show exactly how this arrogance is expressed in each passage.

Azaria is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it functions as an individual’s name. The name appears 18 times in 18 verses, from 2 Kings through Daniel, including genealogical and historical passages. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning in the text is the personal name “Azaria.”

Aia is a proper name, also represented as Ea. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament, across passages in 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the specific person or place identified in each occurrence cannot be determined from the name alone.

“Thorny” describes something associated with or covered in thorns. As an adjective, the word identifies a plant or object by its prickly character rather than naming the thorns themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 34:13, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in that passage depends on the context in which the adjective appears.

This word means “involuntarily”: something done without intending or choosing to do it. As an adverb, it describes the manner in which an action happens, emphasizing that the person did not act deliberately. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 16 times, especially in passages addressing actions or wrongs that were not planned. The surrounding passage determines what action is being described, but the word itself points to a lack of deliberate intent.

This Greek LXX adverb means “without trial; unjustly.” It describes an action done without a proper judgment or fair legal process, and therefore done unjustly. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains action carried out without rightful examination or justice.

Aliphalat, also given as Alifalat, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 8:13. The available lexical information identifies it as a name, but does not provide a broader meaning or description beyond that name. Its particular significance in Ezra depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Allon is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears as the personal name “Allon.” The name occurs 11 times in this Greek corpus, across passages from Genesis, Numbers, 1 Chronicles, Daniel, Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and Susanna. Its exact reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a name.

This Greek LXX verb means “mix up” or “mix together.” It describes separate things being combined so that they become mingled rather than remaining distinct. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, across Esther, Ezekiel, and Daniel. Its central idea is combination or intermingling, while the surrounding sentence determines what things are being mixed. It can therefore describe a physical mixture or the joining of distinct groups or elements.

This adjective means “unpurified; impure.” It describes something regarded as still lacking purification, rather than something that has been purified. As an adjective, it characterizes a person, object, or condition, while the surrounding sentence identifies what is being described. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Leviticus 19:23. Its precise force there must be understood from that verse and its surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX adjective means “carrying away.” It describes something connected with taking or bearing something away, rather than naming the action as a verb. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Leviticus 16, in verses 8 and 10. Its precise force in either verse depends on the noun it describes and the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains connected with carrying away.

This adjective means “fitting” or “harmonious,” describing something that suits its purpose or forms a pleasing agreement. It presents the quality of being well-matched, orderly, or in accord rather than awkward or conflicting. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 16:20. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense is something appropriately arranged or united in harmony.

Arsakes, also rendered Arsakis, is a proper name referring to a person named Arsakes in the Greek LXX text. It is not a general description, action, or quality, but an identifying personal name. The name occurs three times, all in 1 Maccabees, appearing in 1 Maccabees 14:2, 14:3, and 15:22. The surrounding passages are needed to identify the person’s specific role or significance in each mention.

Askalon is the name of a place, referring to the ancient city of Ashkelon. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, this proper name identifies that location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It appears 20 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. The name occurs in passages associated with Israel’s history and with surrounding nations, but its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

“Near” is an adjective describing something located close by or nearby. It identifies a person or thing by closeness rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, this word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:8. That reference marks its only recorded occurrence; the surrounding verse text would be needed to determine exactly what is described as near in that passage.

This adjective means “obscure”: something not easily seen, recognized, understood, or brought into clear notice. It describes what is hidden from ordinary view or lacks public prominence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including in Job, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one passage depends on what the surrounding sentence says about the person, thing, or matter being described.

This word means “abruptly”: it describes something happening suddenly, without warning or gradual preparation. As an adverb, it tells how an action or event occurs rather than naming the action itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, it occurs ten times, including passages in Joshua, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah, and the Maccabean books. Its central idea remains a sharp, unexpected change or event. The precise force in any individual verse depends on the action and surrounding sentence.

Baithbasi, also rendered Vethvasi, is a proper name rather than a general description or action. It identifies a named person, place, or other specific referent, but the available wording does not establish which kind of referent it is. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs twice, both in 1 Maccabees 9, at verses 62 and 64. Its precise reference must therefore be understood from the surrounding text in each passage.

This LXX noun means “royal,” describing something connected with a king, kingdom, or royal status. It identifies what belongs to or is associated with kingship rather than naming an ordinary object or person in general. The word occurs 27 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is established across several settings, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what royal thing is being described.

“Boua” is a proper name, also rendered “Vua.” It functions as a name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 2:60. Its lexical meaning is limited to the name itself, so its precise identity and significance must be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

This adjective describes something as “living in the deep,” referring to life found in deep waters. It is a descriptive word rather than a name or action, so it identifies where a living creature belongs or exists. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 6:8. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is life associated with the depths.

Giezi is a proper name referring to a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but a personal designation. In this corpus, the name occurs 14 times, all in 2 Kings, across 13 verses. Its recorded use begins in 2 Kings 4 and continues through 2 Kings 8. The English rendering preserves it as “Giezi,” reflecting its function as a personal name rather than translating it as an ordinary descriptive term.

This Greek LXX verb means “fear”: to experience fear or to regard something with fear. It describes an inner response that can be expressed as being afraid. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, appearing seven times in Job and once in Isaiah. Its wording can describe a person’s fear or the fearful response associated with creatures and circumstances. The surrounding verse determines what causes the fear and how strongly it is felt.

This noun refers to the passing or course of life—the way a person’s life proceeds. It can describe life’s journey or manner of living rather than a single moment or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther.3.13. The related idea of a “way” points to a life understood as a path or ongoing course. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning concerns the course or passing of life.

This adverb means “continually” or “constantly,” describing something that continues without stopping or happens repeatedly. It answers the question of how long or how regularly an action takes place, rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: once in Esther and three times in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the action or condition it modifies.

This word means “pole running through rings; stave,” referring to a sturdy rod used to support or carry an object. It is a noun describing a physical part of the tabernacle furnishings and their carrying equipment. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in Exodus, in passages concerning construction, arrangement, or transport of the sanctuary furnishings. Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding description, but its basic meaning remains a pole or stave fitted through rings.

This word means “giver”: a person who gives something to another. As a noun, it identifies the one who provides or bestows rather than the thing given or the act of giving. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Proverbs 22:8. Its basic meaning remains focused on the person who gives; the surrounding verse determines what is given and what further significance the word has in that passage.

This noun refers to sunset or the west—the direction where the sun goes down. It can describe the time of day when daylight ends, or identify the western direction. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 54 times, showing that both time-related and directional uses are established. Its exact sense in a particular verse is determined by whether the surrounding sentence speaks about a time or a place.

This Greek LXX noun means “knowledge”—awareness or understanding of something. It names what a person knows rather than describing an action. The word occurs once in the Greek text represented here, in Sirach 42:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains knowledge: informed awareness that can be possessed, recognized, or expressed. This is a distinct Greek LXX word and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament lexical entry.

This noun means “abandonment”—the act or condition of being left behind or forsaken. It names the withdrawal or departure of someone or something rather than describing an action as a verb. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 23 times across 23 verses, showing that it is used in varied passages while retaining this central idea. The surrounding words and verse determine who or what is abandoned and what the abandonment involves.

This noun means “exercise; practice”: repeated effort undertaken to develop or maintain a skill or discipline. It describes an activity viewed as training rather than as a single achievement. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Wisdom 13:10. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, since the verse text is not included here. Its basic sense remains focused on deliberate practice or training.

This Greek LXX verb means “blow up.” It describes the act of causing something to swell, burst, or become expanded, though the exact sense in a particular passage depends on its surrounding context. The word occurs 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is used more than rarely but remains tied to specific actions rather than a broad abstract idea. Its normal function is to express an action performed or taking place.

This Greek LXX verb means “fly away”—to leave by taking flight or move swiftly away. It describes an action rather than a person or thing, so it tells what someone or something does. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, in Proverbs 7:10. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is departure through flight or rapid movement away.

This noun means “foreigner” or “immigrant,” referring to someone who has come from another place and lives among people who are native to the land. It identifies a person by their outsider or newcomer status rather than by an occupation or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Job 20:26. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a person who is not originally from the place where they are living.

This Greek LXX verb means “recognize” or “find out.” It describes coming to know someone or something clearly, whether through recognition or through discovering information. The word appears 130 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is used broadly for gaining definite knowledge rather than merely noticing something. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “viceroy,” a noun for an official who governs with authority delegated by a higher ruler. It identifies a person holding a senior governing position rather than an ordinary messenger or servant. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:38. The word’s precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to a ruler’s representative or deputy.

This verb means “sing,” describing the act of expressing words or melody in song. It functions as an action word rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 1:30. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is the act of singing.

This word means “stores,” referring to supplies or goods kept for use. It is a noun, so it names the stored things rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both in 1 Chronicles 26, indicating a narrowly used term within this corpus. Its basic meaning remains the stored provisions or goods themselves; the surrounding verse determines exactly what kind of stores are intended.

This LXX verb means “test,” describing the act of examining or putting something to the proof. It can refer to investigating what is true, sincere, or reliable rather than merely observing it. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, including passages from Genesis, Chronicles, Esther, Job, and Susanna. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what—or whom—is being examined, but its central idea remains deliberate testing or examination.

This word means “celebrate” or “cheer,” describing gladness expressed openly. It is a verb, so it points to the action of rejoicing rather than merely an inward feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly—232 times across 219 verses—including passages connected with worship, festivals, praise, and glad response. Its central idea is active joy: people may celebrate, or someone may cheer others, in response to God’s goodness or a joyful occasion.

This noun refers to an approach or coming—the act of drawing near or arriving. It can describe someone’s arrival, the movement toward a place, or the onset of an event. The word appears nine times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, all in 1 and 2 Maccabees. Its central sense remains straightforward: something or someone is coming toward a person or place. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the arrival itself or on the approaching movement.

Zabouthaithan is a proper name, rendered as “Zabouthaithan” or “Zavuthethan.” It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Esther 9:9. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, this entry supports identifying the name and its spelling variants, but does not establish whether it names a person, place, or another named entity.

This noun means “tranquility; quiet,” describing a state of calm or stillness rather than disturbance. It can refer to peaceful conditions or a settled state, depending on the sentence in which it appears. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical books, including passages in Joshua, Job, Proverbs, Esther, and 1–2 Maccabees. Its basic idea remains a condition of quietness and calm.

This Greek LXX verb means “defeat”: to overcome or cause an opponent to lose. It describes the action of defeating someone or something rather than merely facing opposition. The word occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, with most occurrences in Isaiah and other prophetic or historical passages. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on who is defeated and how the surrounding sentence describes that defeat.

This noun refers to “his guidance”—the direction or leading associated with him. It names guidance as something a person has or follows, rather than describing an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Job 37:12. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its lexical sense is clear: guidance belonging to or coming from him.

Thilon is a proper name, referring to a person named Thilōn. It is not presented as an ordinary descriptive word, action, or quality, so its significance here is its role as a personal name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:20. The available information identifies the name but does not provide a further meaning or explanation of the person’s role. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage.

This word denotes the number eleven and is also identified with “kaph.” It functions as an indeclinable number, so it serves as a fixed numerical designation rather than describing an action, person, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Psalms 118:81. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so its exact role in that occurrence cannot be described further.

This noun means “altar at the right side.” It identifies an altar by its position, distinguishing it as the one located on the right side. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Kings 12:10, so it functions as a specific designation rather than a broad term used throughout the biblical text. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and temple description, but its lexical meaning directly points to an altar identified by location.

This adjective means “his own” or “private,” describing something belonging to a person or kept as that person’s particular possession or concern. It can identify what is personally one’s own rather than shared or public. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 53 times, so its exact English wording may vary with the noun or situation it describes. Its central idea remains personal ownership, distinction, or privacy.

Iephtha, also rendered Ieftha, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 10:3. Because it is a proper name, its meaning lies primarily in identifying a particular person, and its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative. The name itself does not provide a general command, promise, or spiritual quality.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iōsaias” or “Ioseas.” It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 26:25. The available lexical meaning identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain which person bears it or what role that person has in the passage.

Kamin is a proper name rendered “Kamin.” It identifies a named person, place, or other specific entity rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 21:38. The available lexical information establishes the name itself, while the surrounding verse would be needed to determine exactly what named entity Kamin identifies in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means to wound someone severely or to spoil something utterly. It describes serious damage, whether directed against a person or resulting in complete ruin. The word appears six times, all in 4 Maccabees, so its normal sense is concentrated in that book’s language rather than spread broadly across the Greek Old Testament. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being damaged and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX noun means a lodger or guest—a person staying in a place without being its permanent resident. It can describe someone received into another person’s home or community for a time. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Wisdom 5:14, and is rendered “guest” there. Its basic sense therefore points to temporary residence and the status of one who is present as a welcomed visitor rather than an established inhabitant.

This noun refers to cursing—the pronouncing or expressing of a curse. It names an act or expression of invoking harm, judgment, or misfortune rather than describing a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Numbers and once in Jeremiah. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the act of cursing. The word is distinct from English translation choices and is best understood through this central sense.

This verb means “applaud” or “extol,” describing speech or action that openly praises and honors someone. It expresses favorable approval rather than criticism or rejection. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 7:13. Because the verse text is not included here, the precise force of the praise in that passage depends on its surrounding context, but the word itself points to active commendation or exaltation.

Kis is a proper name, used to identify a person rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 20 times across 16 verses. The name occurs especially in genealogical and historical passages, including references in 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, and 2 Chronicles. Its precise identification in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogy.

This Greek LXX noun means “sexual intercourse,” referring plainly to sexual relations. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Leviticus 20:15. Because the word itself names the act rather than a person or a moral quality, its precise force in that passage comes from the surrounding legal statement. The term therefore gives a direct description of sexual relations, while the passage in which it appears determines how that act is addressed there.

This word means “ram,” a mature male sheep. It is a noun used for the animal itself, including rams brought as offerings or used in sacrificial settings. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 173 times, with especially frequent use in Numbers, Leviticus, and Exodus. Its meaning remains straightforward: it identifies a ram rather than sheep generally or another sacrificial animal. The surrounding passage determines the ram’s particular role, but the word itself names the animal.

Lamech is a proper name referring to people named Lamech in the Old Testament. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears eleven times in ten verses, beginning in Genesis and appearing again in 1 Chronicles. Genesis mentions Lamech in two family lines, so the name identifies more than one person rather than expressing a general quality or action. Its meaning here is simply the personal name “Lamech,” also rendered “Lamekh.”

Louith, also written Loith, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person, place, or other subject rather than expressing an ordinary action or quality. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Isaiah 15:5. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, the specific subject identified by the name cannot be determined here; the secure meaning is the name itself and its recognized alternate rendering.

Maragella is a proper name—the name “Maragella,” also rendered “Marayella.” As a name, it identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Joshua 19:11. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine the named entity’s significance or the details of its surrounding passage; those require the verse and its context.

This verb means “modulate” or “sing.” It describes producing or shaping musical sound, especially by singing or adjusting a melody. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, so its central sense is clear even though its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding context. The word may refer to vocal music or the deliberate shaping of a tune, rather than simply making an unspecified sound. It is a Greek LXX word used as a verb.

This adjective describes someone who hates virtue—that is, a person opposed to moral goodness. It presents virtue as something the person rejects or resists, rather than something admired and practiced. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 11:4. The reference identifies its only recorded occurrence, while the word’s basic meaning remains “hater of virtue.” Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means to dirty or pollute something, making it unclean or defiled. It describes an action that affects a person, object, place, or condition by introducing uncleanness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 17 times across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic meaning is consistent while the precise object and force depend on the surrounding verse. The word appears in passages ranging from Genesis and Isaiah to Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Sirach, showing its use for different kinds of defilement.

Mosōbab, also rendered Mosovav, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament, with the name appearing once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 4:34. Because personal names are used to identify individuals, the name itself does not provide a general meaning or instruction apart from the person it names. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding text and the individual’s place in the genealogy.

This word means “field-mouse,” referring to a small mouse-like animal. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament translation and occurs once, in Leviticus 11:30. The word identifies the animal itself rather than an action, quality, or person. Since it appears only once and no verse text is provided here, its broader scriptural use cannot be traced beyond this specific animal designation.

This adjective means “newborn,” referring to someone or something that has only recently been born. It describes the condition of being at the earliest stage of life, rather than an older infant or child. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains newly born.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “nest”: it describes nesting or making a nest. Its ordinary sense concerns the place where a bird settles or lives, rather than a broad symbolic idea by itself. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. [p03:word:lxx:L709359:identity; p03:word:lxx:L709359:occurrences; p01:word:lxx:L709359:reference:0]

This verb means to hesitate—to hold back or be slow to act because of uncertainty or reluctance. It describes a person who does not proceed readily, rather than directly expressing refusal. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, appearing in Numbers, Judges, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what the surrounding passage shows about the person’s reason for delaying or holding back.

This Greek LXX adjective describes someone bearing arms—an armed warrior or soldier. It identifies a person by military readiness or role rather than by a place, object, or action. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Chronicles 14:7. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, its exact force in that sentence cannot be expanded beyond this basic sense. Its central idea is a person equipped to fight or serve as an armed soldier.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something firm, strong, or lasting—something that remains established rather than easily giving way. Its central sense is “firm; lasting,” and it can describe structures, defenses, or other things marked by durability. The word occurs 61 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing repeated use for what is secure or enduring. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This LXX noun expresses the idea of being “in full array,” describing something arranged or present as a complete whole. Its sense emphasizes completeness rather than a partial selection. It appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 3:12. The lexical meaning identifies the word’s central sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain what is arranged or fully present there.

This verb means to bind something up or twine it around something else. It describes an action of wrapping, winding, or fastening rather than a feeling, quality, or object. The word appears once in the Greek text represented here, in 3 Maccabees 2:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the joining or encircling of something by binding it around.

This noun means “bitterness,” naming a bitter condition or quality. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, appearing 26 times in this LXX corpus. The word occurs across books such as Exodus, Deuteronomy, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Sirach, showing that it describes a recurring scriptural idea rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

gl: he who has the spirit; bearer of the spirit
d: he who has the spirit; bearer of the spirit

e.t: This noun refers to “he who has the spirit” or a “bearer of the spirit.” It describes a person characterized by possessing or carrying the spirit, rather than naming an action or quality by itself. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Hosea and once in Zephaniah. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains a person who has or bears the spirit.

This verb means “prostitute; depraved,” describing prostitution or depraved conduct. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it appears 17 times across 17 verses, so it is a recurring action word rather than a rare title or name. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject, but its central sense remains connected with prostitution or moral depravity.

Provision means what is supplied or arranged to meet a need. As a noun, it points to an act, resource, or preparation made for someone’s support or benefit. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs nine times, appearing once in the Old Testament material and eight times in deuterocanonical books. Its central idea remains the supplying or arranging of what is needed, while the surrounding verse determines who provides it and what need is being addressed.

This Greek LXX verb means “step up to,” describing movement toward or onto a higher place or position. It focuses on approaching by going upward, rather than simply arriving. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, including descriptions of boundaries and places in Exodus and Joshua. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains upward movement toward something.

This word means “earlier”. It points to something that happened before another time, event, or point of reference. As an adjective or adverb, it can describe what came first or indicate a previous occasion. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 60 times, showing a recurring way to mark sequence in time. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what earlier event or time the surrounding passage is discussing.

This Greek LXX noun means “stem,” referring to the supporting lower part of a plant. It names the part from which a plant’s branches, leaves, or growth arise, rather than the whole plant itself. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX data, appearing in Genesis and Proverbs. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains the stem or base of a plant.

This word means “roam”: to move about without staying in one settled place. It is a verb, describing an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 7:12, so its wider range of use cannot be established from repeated passages. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but the central idea is movement from place to place without a fixed location.

Saphath, also rendered Safath, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it identifies a person by name and occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 3:22. The available rendering preserves the name as “Saphath,” so its meaning is chiefly its function as an individual’s designation. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s place in the genealogy or narrative.

Siba, also rendered Siva, is a proper name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named Siba. The name occurs 16 times across 13 verses, all in 2 Samuel, from 2 Samuel 9 through 2 Samuel 19. Its meaning is therefore its personal identification: it distinguishes this particular man within the narrative. The surrounding passage is needed to explain his specific role in any individual verse.

This Greek LXX noun means “pale.” It identifies something characterized by a pale or light appearance. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus: three times in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its recorded occurrences are in Numbers 33:55, Ezekiel 28:24, Hosea 2:8, and Sirach 43:19. The precise force of the noun in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This adjective means “wise,” describing someone marked by good judgment, understanding, and skill in handling life rightly. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used broadly for people regarded as wise, and it can also describe wisdom expressed in speech or conduct. The word occurs 178 times in this corpus, with especially frequent use in Proverbs, where wisdom is presented as a practical way of living rather than merely possessing information. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “herald of the army,” referring to a person who publicly announces a military message or command. It presents the speaker as an official messenger connected with an army, rather than simply someone who delivers ordinary news. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at 1 Kings 22:36. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a military herald or announcer.

This adjective describes things that are mixed together or people involved in promiscuous unions. Its central idea is lack of separation: what should remain distinct has become mingled. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 2:43. Because the word is an adjective, it describes a person or thing rather than naming an action by itself. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is “commingled; promiscuous.”

This noun describes someone sitting with others in council. It points to participation in a council setting rather than merely being seated alone. The core idea is a person who sits alongside others as part of a deliberating group. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs two times, including one occurrence in Judges and one in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning centers on sitting together in council.

This word means a “gathering; meeting of people.” It is a noun for people coming together in one place, emphasizing the assembled group rather than a private meeting or solitary action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within Judges 9:46 and 9:49. Its ordinary sense is therefore straightforward: a gathering or assembly of people. The surrounding passage determines what the gathering is for, but the word itself identifies the meeting of people as a group.

Sosipatros is a proper name—the personal name of an individual, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees: 12:19 and 12:24. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the surrounding verse text, its particular role in each passage must be understood from those contexts. The name itself remains Sosipatros in both occurrences.

This Greek noun means “wall”: a built structure that encloses, separates, or protects a place. It is used for city walls, house walls, and other boundary structures. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 175 times, showing that it is a common word for a physical barrier or fortification. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from whether the surrounding passage emphasizes defense, separation, enclosure, or the breaking down of a wall.

This noun means “honor” or “value”: the worth given to a person, thing, or matter, and the recognition or esteem that worth deserves. It can therefore refer either to valued status or to an assessed worth, depending on the sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 69 times, so it is a broadly used term rather than a rare expression. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on what is being honored or valued and on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX verb means “traumatize”: to inflict a serious wound or injury. As a verb, it describes an action done to someone rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages from 1 Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Song of Songs. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on physical injury or its painful result, but the central idea remains the infliction of a wound.

This noun means “gatherer of grapes,” referring to a person who collects grapes during the harvest. It names an agricultural worker rather than the grapes, the vineyard, or the act of gathering itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Jeremiah and Obadiah, so its meaning remains focused and specific rather than broad or figurative. The surrounding verse determines what is being said about such a person in each passage, but the word itself identifies someone engaged in gathering grapes.

This Greek LXX verb means “overpower”: to prevail over someone or something through greater strength or force. It describes an action rather than a person or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at 1 Kings 16:22. Its basic sense is clear, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that overcoming is expressed in that passage.

This adjective means “bald” or “baldheaded,” describing someone whose head lacks hair. It refers to a physical appearance rather than an action or inward quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, across Leviticus, 2 Kings, and Ezekiel. The wording is rendered “bald” where an English rendering is available, supporting the straightforward sense of the word. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Phelōthi is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It is also rendered “Felothi,” giving two forms of the same personal name. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 2 Samuel 23:26. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself identifies someone but does not tell us that person’s role or significance in the passage.

This word is a proper name rendered “Phrourai; Frure.” It identifies a named person, place, group, or designation in the Greek Old Testament text, rather than describing an ordinary action or quality. The word occurs five times, all within Esther, from Esther 9:26 through Esther 10:3. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its exact referent in each occurrence cannot be specified here. Its meaning is therefore best retained as the proper name “Phrourai; Frure.”

This word is a proper name rendered “Chettaia” or “Khettea.” It identifies a named person or group in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. It occurs three times in the LXX, in 1 Kings 11:1 and Ezekiel 16:3, 45. The precise individual or referent is determined by the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a name.

This noun refers to light, dry material such as chaff or powder. It names something easily scattered, crushed, or dispersed rather than something solid and enduring. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Isaiah, so its meaning is established within a narrow set of passages. The word’s basic sense remains material and concrete; the surrounding verse determines what comparison or picture it contributes there. It is rendered “powder” in one recorded English rendering, alongside the broader lexical sense “chaff.”

This Greek LXX verb means “play,” describing the act of producing music or playing an instrument. It is an action word rather than a name for the instrument or the performer. The word occurs 35 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, most often in Psalms, where its musical use is especially common. Its basic sense remains the activity of playing, while the surrounding verse determines what is being played and for what purpose.

Ōrōnitou, also rendered Oronitu, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament, specifically in the book of Nehemiah. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Nehemiah 13:28. The available lexical information identifies it as a proper noun, so its role is to name a person; its precise significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.
